item.title: The Fold — 2026-11-19
item.description: The Fold morning briefing for 19 November 2026: Xi Jinping, Donald Trump, and Vladimir Putin hold their first trilateral summit in Shenzhen as Ukraine strikes the Kerch Bridge for a third time and Elon Musk disavows MAGA, Brussels warns Andy Burnham to decide on reversing Brexit as the Iran war drives UK inflation to 3.6% and energy bills toward £2,166, Brazil's Federal Police deliver Banco Master reports on Supreme Court justices to Edson Fachin, Anthropic prices its Nasdaq IPO at $83 for a $1.5 trillion valuation, Grand Theft Auto VI launches to a record-tying 99 Metacritic score as a Van Gogh fetches $190.4 million, and Mauricio Pochettino takes charge of relegation-threatened Manchester United.
item.content:encoded:
Thursday 19 November 2026 · London

The Fold

Your morning briefing from the UK & the world

In this edition

  • Xi Jinping, Donald Trump, and Vladimir Putin hold their first trilateral summit in Shenzhen as Ukraine strikes the Kerch Bridge for a third time and Elon Musk declares he has left the MAGA movement behind.
  • European capitals warn Andy Burnham they will shut the door on long-term talks until Britain decides whether to reverse Brexit, while fuel prices from the Iran war push UK inflation to 3.6 per cent and January energy bills toward £2,166.
  • Brazil’s Federal Police deliver confidential reports on Supreme Court justices’ ties to Banco Master owner Daniel Vorcaro as the Senate delays its fiscal adjustment vote and prosecutors indict Flávio Bolsonaro for slander.
  • Anthropic prices its Nasdaq debut at $83 a share for a valuation of up to $1.5 trillion as US Democrats probe Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s family stake in Nvidia and Google rolls out Gemini 4 Neon.
  • Grand Theft Auto VI launches worldwide to a record-tying 99 Metacritic average and console network outages, Sotheby’s auctions an 1890 Vincent van Gogh canvas for $190.4 million, and Glastonbury unveils its youngest headliner trio of the century.
  • Mauricio Pochettino begins work at relegation-threatened Manchester United ahead of Sunday’s trip to Anfield as Chelsea beat Paris Saint-Germain in the Women’s Champions League and Netflix battles Fox in a $2 billion auction for the 2030 World Cup.

News

Xi, Trump and Putin hold historic Shenzhen trilateral as Ukraine strikes Kerch Bridge again and Musk disavows MAGA

Xi Jinping, Donald Trump, and Vladimir Putin sit down in Shenzhen today for the first trilateral meeting ever held between the presidents of China, the United States, and Russia, a gathering that has drawn anxious comparisons across Europe to the 1945 Yalta conference. Xi set the stage on Wednesday by breaking decades of Chinese protocol to greet Trump on the airport tarmac with an embrace—prompting Trump to call his host an “incredible leader”—before standing between his American and Russian counterparts for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) group photograph after Canadian and Australian delegates shelved threatened boycotts. In his keynote address, Xi cast Beijing as the defender of open supply chains against rampant protectionism even as Washington restricted Chinese firms from renting US artificial intelligence chips overseas, while Putin dismissed Western powers as “former hegemons” and declared Europe to be in a “humiliating decline” ahead of today’s talks on Ukraine, the US war in Iran, nuclear arms, and trade. (Guardian, Guardian, BBC)

Hours before the Shenzhen talks began, Ukrainian forces struck the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea for the third time this week. Moscow-installed governor Sergei Aksyonov halted all remaining traffic early on Thursday to assess fresh damage to the crossing, where a seven-stage Ukrainian drone and Flamingo cruise-missile attack had already dropped a 227-metre road span into the Black Sea on Tuesday, while Russian drones killed three civilians in Odesa. After visiting wounded veterans in Lviv, Prince Harry told the Telegraph that Europe had been in an undeclared war with Moscow for a decade and said he would rejoin the British Army if needed. Speaking by video from China to the New York Times DealBook Summit, SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk accused Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of lying about Pentagon-controlled Starshield disruptions and misusing civilian Starlink terminals for offensive drone strikes, saying he refused to make “kill decisions”. In the same interview, Musk declared “I’m not MAGA”, backed split party control in Washington, and admitted he felt “pretty foolish” after spending a record $446 million (£339 million) to back Republicans in last week’s midterms only for Democrats to sweep Congress. (Guardian, BBC, BBC, The Verge, Guardian, BBC)

In the Middle East, Israeli tanks crossed the “yellow line” along central Gaza’s Salah al-Din road into Nuseirat on Wednesday in the military’s first ground incursion into Hamas-controlled territory since October’s ceasefire, displacing families from tent camps a day after the US-backed Board of Peace accused both sides of truce breaches. The raid came as opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot worked to form an Israeli government without caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, while Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara froze building tenders for the E1 West Bank settlement days after UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband sanctioned eight Israeli construction firms. Elsewhere, the International Court of Justice rules today in The Gambia’s seven-year genocide case against Myanmar over the 2017 Rohingya massacres—potentially the first conviction of a state under the 1948 Genocide Convention—and a Miami federal jury convicted pastor Christian Emmanuel Sanon over the 2021 assassination of Haitian President Jovenel Moïse. At COP31, Panamanian Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro warned that the world was “held hostage by the petroleum mafia” as 30 nations backed a separate fossil fuel treaty, while the UN Population Fund found that one in four women globally—and 45 per cent in west and central Africa—cannot refuse sex within marriage. (Guardian, BBC, Guardian, BBC, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

Brussels presses Burnham for Brexit clarity as Iran war drives UK inflation to 3.6% and energy bills toward £2,166

European Union capitals have warned Downing Street that they will shut the door to further long-term negotiations after Friday’s Brussels summit until Prime Minister Andy Burnham decides whether Britain wants to reverse Brexit. Diplomats said member states had tired of piecemeal “reset” summits and wanted a durable cross-party British consensus before investing further effort. While Friday’s joint statement will advance talks on the EU single energy market, irregular migration, and defence, a leaked draft shows friction over Brussels’s demand that London align with EU tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles to qualify for Made in Europe industrial rules. Burnham plans to launch a “national conversation” on Europe next week, even as pro-rejoin MPs worry they have been outflanked by the launch on X of Stay Out—a resurrected Leave campaign claiming rejoining would cost £750 million a week—and after a bruising Prime Minister’s Questions clash with Kemi Badenoch further dented Burnham’s promise of consensual politics. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

At home, oil and gas price shocks from the war in Iran pushed UK consumer price inflation from 3.5 per cent in September to a one-year high of 3.6 per cent in October. Office for National Statistics data showed annual motor fuel inflation jumping 33.2 per cent—the steepest rise since July 2022—as petrol reached a four-year high of 174.7p a litre and diesel hit 199.5p, the highest price since records began in 1996. Ahead of next Wednesday’s Ofgem announcement, consultancy Cornwall Insight forecast that typical dual-fuel energy bills in Great Britain will surge 26 per cent in January to £2,166 a year, adding £443 to household costs and dwarfing Chancellor John Healey’s £100 winter payment for 20 million homes. In Parliament today, Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook introduces the Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill to ban virtually all new leasehold flats in England and Wales in favour of resident-owned commonhold and cap existing annual ground rents at £250 from 2028 before reducing them to a peppercorn rate after 40 years. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, BBC)

Two prominent British legal cases also saw major disclosures today. The Marine Accident Investigation Branch’s final report into the August 2024 sinking of the 56-metre superyacht Bayesian off Porticello, Sicily—which killed software tycoon Mike Lynch, his 18-year-old daughter Hannah, Jonathan and Judy Bloomer, Chris and Neda Morvillo, and chef Recaldo Thomas—concluded that an unforecast 70-knot (80mph) thunderstorm downburst knocked the yacht flat in under 15 seconds and sank it in 18 minutes, and that onboard stability documents never warned the crew of its vulnerability at anchor with sails down and the centreboard raised. Separately, an investigation revealed that paediatric endocrinologist Professor Peter Hindmarsh—the prosecution’s key expert witness arguing that nurse Lucy Letby poisoned babies with insulin—was barred from clinical practice by University College London Hospitals Trust in March 2023, five months before the verdicts, over fears his insulin advice posed an unacceptable risk to child patients. Neither Letby’s defence nor the jury was told of his exclusion or an April 2023 tribunal supervision order. (Guardian, BBC, Guardian)

Elsewhere in Whitehall and the courts, Google refused a Prison Service request to remove a YouTube video in which Laura Brand read a prison message from her husband Russell Brand protesting his innocence after his ten-and-a-half-year sentence for rape and sexual assault. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood backed banning uniformed police from marching in Pride parades under her new impartiality standard, arguing that gender-identity debates made uniformed participation look political—remarks City of London Police Deputy Commissioner Nik Adams warned made LGBTQ+ people feel less safe. In Birmingham, High Court Judge Emma Kelly granted an interim injunction barring anti-migrant group Raise the Colours from hanging flags on council lampposts, hours before a Stafford jury convicted 36-year-old group member Billy Allison of murdering Matthew O’Gara with an unprovoked punch in Lichfield. Meanwhile, a judge rejected McDonald’s bid to strike out harassment claims by hundreds of workers alleging managers failed to protect teenage staff. (BBC, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, BBC)

Federal Police hand Banco Master files on Supreme Court justices to Fachin as Brazil’s Senate stalls on fiscal package

Federal Police (PF) Director-General Andrei Rodrigues delivered the confidential reports detailing links between former Banco Master owner Daniel Vorcaro and Supreme Federal Court (STF) justices to Court President Edson Fachin on Wednesday evening. Fachin immediately forwarded the sealed files to the Prosecutor-General’s Office (PGR) with a 15-day review deadline—an awkward step given that Prosecutor-General Paulo Gonet appears in Vorcaro’s messages and was photographed smoking cigars and drinking whisky with the banker in London in April 2024, though the Federal Public Ministry council voted 5–4 in September against investigating him. Testifying before a joint congressional hearing, Rodrigues defended removing the delegates who wrote the reports and opening a leak probe, arguing they overstepped STF limits by investigating justices without authorisation and risked nullifying the case. Hours earlier, leaked audio from Vorcaro’s phone revealed his lawyer Walfrido Warde boasting of inside information on Rodrigues’s actions in a São Paulo PF inquiry into alleged Gafisa and Banco Master market manipulation—a claim Rodrigues denied. (Folha, Folha, Folha, Meio)

In Congress, Senate President Davi Alcolumbre and rapporteur Eduardo Braga postponed the final vote on four amendments to Planning Minister Bruno Moretti’s R$46 billion-to-R$56 billion fiscal bill after coalition absences threatened a defeat over corporate tax-credit caps. Business groups also warned that trimming the Workers’ Food Programme (PAT) corporate tax deduction from 3.6 per cent to 3.2 per cent—a R$300 million clawback—could prompt employers to drop meal vouchers used by 22 million workers. After low turnout at Tuesday’s protests with the National Union of Students, PSOL leaders Juliano Medeiros, Manuela D’Ávila, and Pastor Henrique Vieira ruled out further rallies and reined in radical critics such as incoming deputy Jones Manoel, while the Human Rights Ministry cancelled a R$722,000 staff massage tender. Meanwhile, Workers’ Party chief Edinho Silva opened fourth-term cabinet talks offering União Brasil Regional Development and Tourism while shifting Communications and Science and Technology to the Progressistas (PP), which demanded bigger budgets. (Meio, Meio, Folha, Folha, Folha, Folha)

Speaking at the Buenos Aires Forum alongside Justice Gilmar Mendes, Chamber Speaker Hugo Motta confirmed he and Alcolumbre had asked Justice Alexandre de Moraes to schedule the constitutional actions on the “Dosimetry Law” cutting sentences for Jair Bolsonaro and the 8 January 2023 coup convicts to “turn this page”. Motta’s February re-election bid faces right-wing resistance after Nikolas Ferreira threatened to quit the Liberal Party if it backs him and Novo launched Paulo Martins for speaker; Ferreira also won a federal injunction blocking a Senate tender for 95 iPhone 18 Pro handsets. At the STF, Deputy Prosecutor-General Luiza Frischeisen indicted Senator Flávio Bolsonaro for criminal slander against President Lula over an X post after Nicolás Maduro’s capture linking Lula to drug and arms trafficking. In state politics, Paraná Governor-elect Sergio Moro named former Lava Jato prosecutor Carlos Fernando dos Santos Lima as Anti-Corruption Secretary, while São Paulo Governor Tarcísio de Freitas put “super-secretary” Natália Resende in charge of a new Planning, Budget, and Investments portfolio to tighten oversight of public concessions and kept Osvaldo Nico at Public Security. (Folha, Folha, MacMagazine, Folha, Folha, Folha, Folha)

Technology

Anthropic prices Nasdaq IPO at $83 for $1.5tn valuation as Democrats probe Lutnick’s Nvidia stake and Google launches Gemini 4 Neon

Anthropic priced its initial public offering at $83 a share on Wednesday night—above its $70-to-$78 target range after orders were more than ten times oversubscribed—valuing the five-year-old artificial intelligence firm at up to $1.5 trillion (£1.14 trillion) as it begins trading on the Nasdaq today under the ticker ANT. Chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela Amodei, and five co-founders who left OpenAI over safety disputes in late 2020 will ring the opening bell, each holding a stake above $18 billion and selling $260 million in shares. As the first pure-play generative AI developer to list after Sam Altman delayed OpenAI’s debut, Anthropic tests whether surging revenues can outrun data-centre costs: sales climbed from $41 million in 2023 to $4.59 billion in 2025 and $16.29 billion in the first half of 2026—with analysts forecasting $52 billion this year and $135 billion in 2027—yet half-year net losses hit $80 billion alongside $70 billion in 12-month compute commitments and $900 billion in leases through 2045. (Guardian, BBC, BBC)

That hardware boom is drawing sharp political scrutiny. Senior House Democrats Jamie Raskin, Gregory Meeks, and Sydney Kamlager-Dove demanded answers from Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over whether he compromised US national security during the Nvidia affair to enrich his adult children and Cantor Fitzgerald, the firm he led for decades that held hundreds of millions of dollars in Nvidia stock as the chipmaker’s pure profit reached $8,300 a second. Facing local opposition to power-hungry US server farms, the Trump administration is promoting its “Pax Silica” initiative to build chip fabs and AI data centres in the Philippines, where protesters marched with a prop casket in Manila during Trump’s visit. Meanwhile, the US Justice Department indicted Russian national Igor D’iu for unlawfully entering the country via a Telegram network to spy on Palo Alto employees of defence contractor Palantir. (Guardian, The Verge, The Verge, Guardian)

In enterprise and consumer AI, Google launched Gemini 4 Neon for AI Pro and Ultra subscribers, retiring Gemini 3.1 Pro and Argon with a one-million-token model that matches Gemini 4 Carbon on coding and reasoning at Flash speeds to rank third overall on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. Google’s drive to bundle Gemini sparked a backlash from the New York City, Los Angeles, and Chicago school districts, which are considering dropping Google Search after education vice-president Chris Phillips said schools opting out of AI features next year will lose Search access—a policy criticised by Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Senator Bernie Sanders. On Capitol Hill, Senators Ron Wyden, Ed Markey, and Ben Luján pressed Apple, Google, and Meta over AI “nudify” apps in their stores as lawmakers pushed the DEFIANCE Act and a ban on forced arbitration for online harms. (9to5Mac, The Verge, 9to5Mac, MacMagazine, The Verge)

Across Apple’s platforms, the second developer betas of iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and watchOS 27.3 activated daily usage caps on complex Siri AI queries, added the iPhone’s Siri Visual Intelligence mode to the iPad Camera app, introduced two styles for the Siri Modular watch face, and gave the foldable iPhone Duo front-camera Face Unlock when closed alongside Attention Aware controls—while leaks pointed to a rounded titanium frame and quad-curved display for next year’s 20th-anniversary iPhone 20 Pro alongside an iPhone Duo 2. Apple also shipped HomeView 27.2.1 bug fixes, updated Pages, Numbers, Keynote, Final Cut Pro 13 (with MotionVFX), and Pixelmator Pro under Apple Creator Studio, and named 45 finalists across 13 categories for the 2026 App Store Awards, including Brazilian studio Minimol Games’ Case Solved: The London Files for Apple TV. Elsewhere, Google released Google Wallet for iOS in the US without tap-to-pay, Mac launcher Alfred 6 added a native workflow UI toolkit, MacPaw brought its Moonlock security app to iPhone, OpenAI lifted ChatGPT’s ten-minute Live Dictation limit, and Instagram allowed users to edit published Stories for 15 minutes. (9to5Mac, MacStories, 9to5Mac, 9to5Mac, 9to5Mac, 9to5Mac, 9to5Mac, MacMagazine, MacMagazine, MacMagazine, MacMagazine, 9to5Mac, The Verge)

Culture

Grand Theft Auto VI launches to record-tying 99 Metacritic score as Van Gogh sells for $190.4m and Glastonbury names youngest headliners

Thirteen years after its predecessor, Rockstar Games releases Grand Theft Auto VI worldwide today to rave reviews that give the crime epic a 99 out of 100 average on Metacritic—tying Nintendo’s 1998 The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time as the highest-rated video game in history. Critics hailed the fictional Florida state of Leonida and Vice City as the most detailed virtual world ever built, moving seamlessly between bank heists, in-game social-media doomscrolling that reveals side missions, beach walks, and flat-pack furniture assembly, while praising the chemistry of fugitive lovers Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval. That central romance led Rockstar to explain that it removed the series’ option to pick up sex workers so gameplay would remain true to a story about “lovers on the run”. (Guardian, Guardian, BBC, IGN, IGN)

The launch strained digital infrastructure before midnight in Europe and North America. Sony’s PlayStation Network suffered login and download outages on Wednesday evening, while US provider Xfinity reported a fourfold surge in Xbox traffic as players switched console regions to New Zealand for early access, pushing concurrent viewership across Twitch, YouTube, and Kick to a record 6.38 million—nearly four times Valorant’s previous peak. Reclusive Rockstar president Sam Houser issued a rare statement celebrating games as essential modern culture, while benchmarks showed a steady 30 frames per second on PS5 and Xbox Series X with occasional dips to 24fps on Xbox Series S. In Georgia, 43 soldiers in the US Army’s 9th Engineer Battalion at Fort Stewart re-enlisted under an incentive offering four days of paid leave to play the title, while Edinburgh animation programmer Nestor Uriarte urged Rockstar staff to vote yes in this month’s ballot for union recognition. (Guardian, IGN, IGN, IGN, IGN, IGN, Guardian)

In the art market, Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs (Chestnut Trees in Blossom)—painted in Auvers-sur-Oise during the final two months of his life in 1890—sold to dealer William Acquavella at Sotheby’s New York for $190.4 million (£144.9 million), breaking the artist’s $117.2 million record after an eleventh-hour settlement between the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection and the heirs of German Jewish owners the Fischer family over its Nazi-era sale. In British live music, Glastonbury announced the youngest Pyramid Stage headliner trio of the 21st century for June 2027: Sam Fender and Harry Styles (both 33 next summer) make their headline debuts on Friday and Saturday before 25-year-old Billie Eilish closes Sunday, alongside Cher in the Legends slot and a Worthy Farm debut for Kraftwerk. (Guardian, BBC, Guardian)

In film and stage news, Puck reported that The Crown star Josh O’Connor was director Denis Villeneuve’s early favourite for James Bond ahead of Callum Turner and Jack Lowden before O’Connor withdrew after his screen test over the role’s baggage, opening the door for Robert Pattinson. Meanwhile, Florence Pugh rebuked “disturbing” online speculation over her Governors Awards photos by denying cosmetic surgery or Ozempic use; 25-year-old Peruvian rapper Renata Flores is reclaiming the Inca language of Quechua for eight million Andean speakers through urban trap and hip-hop; London critics hailed the National Gallery’s reunion of Jan van Eyck’s oil portraits and Kelly Gough’s performance in Ebenezer Bamgboye’s staging of Eugene O’Neill’s Desire Under the Elms at the Almeida Theatre; and Oxford historian Theodore Zeldin died aged 93. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

Sports

Pochettino takes charge of relegation-threatened Manchester United ahead of Anfield trip as Chelsea beat PSG and Netflix eyes $2bn World Cup deal

Mauricio Pochettino arrived at Manchester United’s Carrington training ground on Wednesday after flying overnight from Cincinnati following his final match in charge of the United States against Haiti, calling his appointment “an honour” and “adrenaline” ahead of Sunday’s Premier League trip to Liverpool at Anfield. As assistants Jesús Pérez, Toni Jiménez, and Sebastiano Pochettino took charge of non-internationals and the 54-year-old Argentinian vowed to challenge Manchester City’s local dominance, United’s position in 18th place after ten games—their first time in the relegation zone at this stage in 40 years, alongside Sunderland and Thomas Frank’s Crystal Palace—drew comparisons with the post-Sir Matt Busby decline that led to their 1974 relegation and warnings that in 19 of 31 Premier League seasons only one of the bottom three after ten games survived. In the US, women’s coach Emma Hayes joined the panel picking Pochettino’s successor, while Opta analysis highlighted how Arsenal full-backs Ben White and Riccardo Calafiori lead all Premier League defensive partnerships with six goal involvements this season. (Guardian, Guardian, BBC, Guardian, Guardian)

In the Women’s Champions League, teenage Dutch defender Veerle Buurman scrambled home a late near-post corner at AFC Wimbledon’s stadium on Wednesday night to give Sonia Bompastor’s Chelsea a 1–0 victory over Paris Saint-Germain and top spot in the league phase. Off the pitch, Netflix and Fox lead a $1.5 billion-to-$2 billion (£1.13 billion-to-£1.5 billion) bidding war ahead of today’s first-round deadline for combined English- and Spanish-language US rights to the 2030 men’s World Cup, with Apple TV, Amazon, Disney, YouTube, DAZN, ESPN, NBCUniversal, and Skydance also circling—and FIFA tender documents revealing that three-minute mid-half hydration breaks with split-screen commercial slots will stay in 2030. Meanwhile, English Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt confirmed the FA explored a legal challenge against Gianni Infantino’s eligibility for a fourth FIFA presidential term in March before concluding a court bid would fail and backing French challenger Philippe Diallo. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, BBC)

The Fold

A daily briefing for Londoners who want the full picture in one place.

item.description: The Fold morning briefing for 18 November 2026: Alan Milburn's 278-page youth unemployment report triggers a union clash over tax cuts and minimum wage rates while the UK-EU youth mobility scheme faces delays until 2030, Ukraine brings down a span of the Kerch Bridge as Xi Jinping opens the APEC summit in Shenzhen and Mary Peltola wins Alaska for the Democrats, markets and left-wing allies rebel against Lula's fiscal package in Brazil, Nvidia doubles revenue while ruling out Jensen Huang's return, Jeff Bezos details Robert Pattinson's James Bond casting as GTA VI sweeps The Game Awards nominations, and Declan Rice signs a new Arsenal deal to 2031.
item.content:encoded:
Wednesday 18 November 2026 · London

The Fold

Your morning briefing from the UK & the world

In this edition

  • Alan Milburn’s 278-page youth unemployment report triggers a union backlash over employer tax cuts and minimum wage brakes, while draft Brussels texts reveal the UK-EU youth mobility scheme may wait until 2030.
  • Ukraine brings down a key span of the Kerch Bridge in a seven-stage missile and drone operation as Xi Jinping opens the APEC summit in Shenzhen and Democrat Mary Peltola wins Alaska’s Senate seat.
  • Investor doubts and left-wing infighting hit President Lula’s R$56 billion fiscal package in Brazil as congressional leaders press Justice Alexandre de Moraes to schedule a vote on reducing Jair Bolsonaro’s sentence.
  • Nvidia doubles quarterly revenue to $115.8 billion while its board rules out reinstating Jensen Huang, California bans Waymo robotaxis from freeways, and Marco Rubio denies a systemic attack behind US tech outages.
  • Jeff Bezos reveals he personally tested five finalists before casting Robert Pattinson as James Bond, the UK music industry hits a record £8.4 billion, and Grand Theft Auto VI sweeps eight Game Awards nominations.
  • Declan Rice agrees a new £300,000-a-week Arsenal contract until 2031 alongside Jurriën Timber as the club mourns 1971 Double winner Peter Storey and Wayne Rooney opens up on his mental health struggles.

News

Milburn youth review sparks union clash over tax cuts and minimum wage as UK-EU mobility scheme faces delay until 2030

Alan Milburn’s 278-page review into the nearly one million 16-to-24-year-olds outside education, employment, or training (NEET) has opened a rift between Downing Street, employers, and trade unions over workers’ rights and youth pay. Calling the report a “watershed moment” with Britain’s NEET rate at 13.5 per cent—the highest in Europe outside Romania—Prime Minister Andy Burnham backed its core plan to shift billions of pounds from incapacity benefits into a Youth Opportunity Service offering training, health support, and placements in return for participation. To encourage hiring, however, the former Labour health secretary urged ministers to double the salary threshold at which employers start paying National Insurance for entry-level under-25 jobs in retail and hospitality, apply a “cautionary principle” to banning zero-hours contracts, and slow rises in youth minimum wage rates. Pointing out that Britain spends 0.1 per cent of GDP on hiring subsidies against 1 per cent in Denmark, Milburn said the package could cut the NEET rate to 6.8 per cent by 2036 and help 440,000 young people into work. TUC general secretary Paul Nowak urged ministers to deliver guaranteed-hours rules without treating young staff as cheap labour, while disability advocates warned that replacing adult health benefits for under-25s creates a two-tier welfare state based on age rather than need. (Guardian, Guardian, BBC, BBC, BBC, Guardian)

Ahead of Burnham’s Brussels summit on Friday with Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa, a draft joint statement circulated to EU ambassadors shows that the new UK-EU youth mobility scheme may wait until 2030 to take full effect. While negotiators expect an agreement in principle this week alongside pacts on food standards and carbon trading, the draft commits both sides to applying the visa deal “no later than 2028” and making places available “no later than January 2030”. Disagreements over whether EU students at UK universities pay home fees or a reduced international rate have been postponed for six months to align with Brussels’s pending Made in Europe industrial bill. After Boris Johnson accused him of wasting his premiership on Brexit, Burnham told Sky News he will set out long-term options for EU ties next month alongside his ten-year economic plan without yet backing a single model, while the CBI urged leaders to prioritise easing post-Brexit work permits for cross-Channel business trips. (Guardian, BBC, BBC, Guardian)

At home, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood tells the police chiefs’ conference in London today that she is launching a fast-track scheme to train 200 potential superintendents a year after a report condemned force leadership as “frankly inadequate”; between 2023 and 2025, zero forces were rated outstanding for leadership and eight serving or former chief constables faced misconduct probes. Mahmood will also unveil a national impartiality standard instructing officers to leave politics to politicians and avoid “misguided attempts at course correction” that fuel claims of two-tier policing. Meanwhile, British counter-terrorism police confirmed that 41-year-old US Army Lieutenant Colonel Brandon Carroll Tyner—arrested on 10 November at Imjin Barracks in Gloucestershire on suspicion of spying for Russia—has been transferred into US military custody following a joint operation with MI5 and the FBI. (Guardian, BBC, Guardian, BBC)

In education and climate policy, Ofqual chief regulator Sir Ian Bauckham warned GCSE and A-level students that using AI in coursework or bringing smart glasses into exams risks “life-altering” disqualification after device cheating hit 2,225 cases in 2025, echoing South Korea’s move to ban smart glasses and check sleeves for 500,000 candidates sitting Thursday’s eight-hour suneung entrance exam. Separately, the Wellcome Trust commissioned ten research teams to track 300,000 British teenagers ahead of the spring 2027 under-16 social media ban. On net zero, the Climate Change Committee warned that weakening the electric vehicle sales mandate would add 8.4 million tonnes of annual carbon emissions next decade and breach legally binding targets, even as Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh joined Spain and Kenya at COP31 in backing international levies on frequent flyers and cryptocurrency transactions. (Guardian, Guardian, BBC, Guardian, Guardian)

Ukraine collapses Kerch Bridge span in seven-stage strike as Xi opens Shenzhen APEC summit and Peltola wins Alaska

A double-arched span of the 12-mile Kerch Bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea now lies on the Black Sea floor after Ukrainian military and Security Service (SBU) units executed a seven-stage operation that overwhelmed Russian defences. After weeks spent degrading radar and air-defence batteries across Crimea, Ukrainian units—including Robert Brovdi’s “Magyar’s Birds” brigade—launched hundreds of long-range attack drones on Monday night. Because mysterious 100mph speed limits were imposed ten days ago on Ukrainian drones using SpaceX’s Pentagon-overseen Starshield network, Kyiv sent a second wave of drones to act as an airborne radio and video relay, guiding at least four Ukrainian-made Flamingo cruise missiles with 1,000kg warheads into the weakened road arch early on Tuesday. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov insisted the crossing Vladimir Putin opened in 2018 would be rebuilt “even better than before”. (Guardian, BBC)

Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping addressed world leaders in Shenzhen today as the APEC summit opened ahead of bilateral meetings with Donald Trump and a three-way US-China-Russia session. Calling for lower trade barriers and deeper artificial intelligence cooperation, Xi projected confidence from China’s hardware capital even as Beijing worries the Nvidia spy scandal will harden US tech curbs. Following intelligence claims that former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang had links to China’s Ministry of State Security during her affair with Jensen Huang, Washington this week restricted Chinese firms from renting US AI chips in third countries such as Malaysia, Thailand, and Brazil. Elsewhere in Asia, Trump’s trade pressure has pushed Tokyo close to lifting its 76-year ban on fresh US table potatoes, alarming Japanese farmers in a country that imports over 60 per cent of its food. (Guardian, BBC, Guardian)

In the United States, Democrat Mary Peltola unseated Republican Senator Dan Sullivan in Alaska on Tuesday—becoming the state’s first Democratic senator since 2008 despite ballot confusion over a second candidate named Dan Sullivan—to complete a nine-seat midterm swing that gives Democrats a 56-seat Senate majority. In federal court, Pakistani national Asif Merchant received a 27-and-a-half-year sentence in Brooklyn for an Iran-linked plot to assassinate Trump in retaliation for Qassem Soleimani’s killing; Manhattan prosecutors charged Irish activist Daithi O’Corrain with using an axe and ball bearings to destroy a $60 million (£45 million) US Air National Guard C-130 Hercules at Shannon Airport; and a judge extended Trump’s deposition deadline in his $10 billion BBC defamation lawsuit to 22 January. Meanwhile, Israel’s Knesset voted 66–52 to elect Matan Kahana—an ally of prime minister-designate Gadi Eisenkot—as speaker to begin unpicking Benjamin Netanyahu’s laws, and lawmakers from Serbia’s anti-corruption Student List danced a traditional kolo outside Belgrade’s parliament before taking their seats after defeating Aleksandar Vučić’s ruling party. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, BBC, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

Market sell-off and left-wing mutiny hit Lula’s fiscal package as Congress presses Moraes to cut Bolsonaro’s sentence

President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva returned to Brasília to face simultaneous rebellions from financial markets and his left-wing base over Planning Minister Bruno Moretti’s R$56 billion fiscal package. Doubts over spending discipline sent the US dollar up 2.15 per cent to R$5.77—making the real the worst performer among 33 currencies—and pushed the Ibovespa down 1.83 per cent as foreign outflows since the runoff hit R$17.5 billion, Morgan Stanley forecast a 7 per cent index drop by 2027, and the Focus survey lifted 2027 inflation expectations to 5 per cent. On the left, activists flooded Congressman André Janones’s pro-Lula WhatsApp channel with scissors emojis—turning the PT’s campaign symbol against Flávio Bolsonaro back onto the government and costing the group 300,000 followers—while PT deputy Lindbergh Farias accused Moretti of authoritarianism and the National Union of Students staged a Rio protest backed by PSOL without the major union confederations. As Moretti met PT deputies to defend an R$18.3 billion cap on corporate tax-credit offsets and Senator Randolfe Rodrigues tabled a Big Tech tax, Lula met PT chief Edinho Silva, Camilo Santana—tipped for Chief of Staff—and Rui Costa to plan his fourth-term cabinet, with Geraldo Alckmin ally Márcio Elias Rosa and Defence secretary-general Cinara Fredo leading contenders to succeed José Múcio at Defence. (Meio, Meio, Folha, Folha, Folha)

At the Supreme Federal Court (STF), Senate President Davi Alcolumbre and Chamber Speaker Hugo Motta met Justice Alexandre de Moraes on Tuesday to urge a plenary vote this year on the congressional “Dosimetry Law” reducing sentences for Jair Bolsonaro and others convicted over the 8 January 2023 coup plot. Moraes indicated he will release the action by the end of the week, and STF President Edson Fachin plans to schedule it promptly—a step supported by fellow justices to defuse opposition amnesty demands, enable Justice Kassio Nunes Marques to rule on Bolsonaro’s release request, and weaken Liberal Party (PL) plans to pursue Moraes’s impeachment next year over his links to former Banco Master owner Daniel Vorcaro. Meanwhile, the 121-strong PL caucus split over Motta’s re-election: while party chief Valdemar Costa Neto feared losing committee chairs that controlled R$8.08 billion in 2026 budget amendments, ideological deputies led by Sóstenes Cavalcante pushed to run Minas Gerais deputy Nikolas Ferreira—history’s most-voted lawmaker with 3.1 million votes—against Motta. (Folha, Folha, Folha)

Final Superior Electoral Court filings showed Lula’s campaign raised R$138.2 million and spent the full R$133.4 million limit—16 per cent above Flávio Bolsonaro’s R$114.6 million—putting the cost per vote at R$2.07 for Lula and R$1.91 for Flávio, with marketing agency Delta3 (R$41 million) and Meta ads (R$17.6 million) leading Lula’s outlays. Separately, the Federal Police concluded its five-year inquiry into R$48.7 million of undelivered Covid-19 ventilators bought by the Northeast Consortium, indicting 17 people including Bruno Dauster and Carlos Eduardo Gabas while clearing former Bahia governor Rui Costa and his wife Aline Peixoto. Elsewhere, Fachin and Moraes inaugurated a sculpture of the double-headed Oxê axe of Yoruba deity Xangô in the STF’s Noble Hall ahead of Black Consciousness Day, and around 20 emaciated members of the isolated Indigenous Awá people emerged from the Amazon in Maranhão seeking food from Guajajara villagers amid illegal logging incursions. (Folha, Folha, Folha, Guardian)

Technology

Nvidia doubles revenue while ruling out Huang’s return as California bans Waymo from freeways and Rubio denies cyber plot

Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of $115.84 billion on Tuesday—doubling sales year-on-year and beating forecasts of $109.15 billion with earnings of $2.68 per share—as board chair Harvey C. Jones ruled out reinstating co-founder Jensen Huang. Hours earlier, Huang issued his first statement since resigning over relationships with direct report Kimberly Powell and former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, telling the Wall Street Journal he would be “honored” to return if asked. Opening the earnings call alongside interim chief executive Colette Kress, Jones said the board had unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation, had no intention of bringing him back, and would take no questions ahead of Huang’s 1 December congressional testimony, sending Nvidia shares up 5 per cent after hours. (Guardian, The Verge, 9to5Mac, BBC)

In artificial intelligence, OpenAI launched GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol for ChatGPT Work and Codex, cutting token use while allowing Astra to replicate slide layouts and typography from screenshots and bringing Sol within half a point of Astra on the FrontierCode 2.0 benchmark at one-fifth the cost. At Microsoft Ignite, chief executive Satya Nadella declared himself “AGI-pilled” on the economic upheaval ahead while backing AI chief Mustafa Suleyman’s warning against Anthropic’s practice of treating models like Claude as potentially conscious beings with moral rights, and Proton released its privacy-focused Lumo Desktop agent. (9to5Mac, MacMagazine, The Verge, MacMagazine)

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and intelligence chief Jay Clayton sought to calm public fears today after a week of tech glitches grounded US flights and disrupted JPMorgan Chase, the National Security Agency, Microsoft Outlook, and Apple’s iCloud, App Store, and Apple Pay. Insisting there was “zero evidence” of a systemic attack, Rubio attributed the failures to routine system patching, while security researcher Scott Helme revealed that hackers compromised web platform Optimizely to inject the Coruna crypto-stealing exploit into 178 major sites—including the BBC, CNN, HSBC, IKEA, and Zoom—targeting unpatched iPhones. On US roads, Alphabet’s Waymo suspended driverless freeway rides nationwide after California’s DMV banned its robotaxis from state highways as an “imminent hazard” following incursions into a Route 101 construction zone and an attempt to overtake highway patrol cars. (BBC, 9to5Mac, 9to5Mac, Guardian, BBC)

For Apple, repair site iFixit criticised the new A18-powered HomeView smart hub after heavy display glue and a chassis-bonded heat shield caused technicians to snap a speaker during teardown, even as Apple detailed the hub’s privacy-isolating Secure Exclaves, added iPhone Duo parts to its Self Service Repair Store, and launched Final Cut Pro 13 with MotionVFX effects. In court, Apple faces a French prosecution brought by campaign group HOP over parts-pairing repair barriers; Epic Games sought daily fines over 122,000 withheld App Store commission documents; and a US judge ruled the government violated the First Amendment by pressuring Apple to remove the ICE-monitoring Eyes Up app. Meanwhile, Apple excluded UK, EU, Brazilian, and South Korean users from iCloud+ Siri AI usage boosts in 2027, and supplier SK Hynix warned that AI memory shortages will keep prices high until 2030. In European business, Modella Capital hired Teneo to auction former WH Smith chain TG Jones—which employs 3,500 people after 150 store closures—and a leak of 15 million files alleged Deutsche Bank ignored compliance warnings over Russian oligarchs and risky clients. (The Verge, MacMagazine, 9to5Mac, MacStories, MacMagazine, 9to5Mac, MacMagazine, MacMagazine, 9to5Mac, Guardian, Guardian)

Culture

Bezos reveals hand in casting Pattinson as Bond while UK music hits £8.4bn and GTA VI sweeps Game Awards nods

Amazon founder Jeff Bezos revealed on Tuesday that he was “heavily involved” in picking Robert Pattinson as the seventh James Bond after paying over $1 billion last year for creative control of the franchise. Speaking at Semafor’s Silicon Valley summit, Bezos admitted he and director Denis Villeneuve were initially biased against the 40-year-old British star because they wanted an unknown actor, until filming three screen-test scenes with each of the five finalists showed Pattinson had “something special”. Meanwhile, critics split sharply over the sixth Hunger Games film, prequel Sunrise on the Reaping—starring Joseph Zada as a teenage Haymitch Abernathy alongside Ralph Fiennes and Kieran Culkin—between praise for its dark commentary and dismissal as an exhausted cash grab. (Guardian, BBC, The Verge, BBC)

In Britain, UK Music’s annual report showed the music industry contributed a record £8.4 billion to the economy in 2025—up 5.7 per cent—as stadium tours by Oasis, Robbie Williams, and Dua Lipa and albums by Olivia Dean lifted exports to £4.8 billion and employment to 220,500, despite warnings over grassroots costs and AI. Addressing similar threats on screen, actors’ union Equity agreed a three-year deal with producers’ body Pact giving 8,000 British performers consent and payment rights over AI “digital replicas”, banning blanket digital-double clauses and strike replacements. Elsewhere, the University of Birmingham paused plans to move the 75-year-old Shakespeare Institute and its 60,000-volume library from Stratford-upon-Avon to Edgbaston after protests led by Dame Judi Dench and the Royal Shakespeare Company. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

On the eve of Thursday’s launch of Grand Theft Auto VI, Rockstar’s crime epic led The Game Awards nominations with eight nods, competing for Game of the Year before reviews have even landed against 007 First Light, Control Resonant, Phantom Blade Zero, Resident Evil Requiem, and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, while Nintendo topped publishers with 12 nominations. The Best Performance list also ended months of secrecy by confirming actress Manni L. Perez as the star playing co-protagonist Lucia Caminos, though Jason Duval’s actor went unnominated. As UK schools offered gift cards to prevent truancy, the Miami Heat unveiled a Vice City NBA court, and fans staged farewell drives through GTA V’s Los Santos, 2K studio Firaxis laid off a third of its staff—around 60 workers—following mixed reviews for Civilization VII, and esports casters protested after Embark Studios replaced human commentators with AI voices in a highlight reel for The Finals. (IGN, IGN, IGN, IGN, IGN, IGN, IGN)

Sports

Declan Rice agrees £300,000-a-week Arsenal deal to 2031 as Gunners mourn Peter Storey and Rooney opens up on mental health

Declan Rice has agreed a new five-year Arsenal contract until 2031 worth around £300,000 a week, matching Bukayo Saka as the joint highest-paid player at the Premier League champions. Signed from West Ham for a club-record £105 million in July 2023 on a £250,000-a-week deal, the 27-year-old midfielder was a driving force in ending Arsenal’s 22-year title wait in May despite second-half back and hamstring injuries, and returned to peak form to win his 82nd England cap against Spain on Sunday. Mikel Arteta’s side also agreed a contract extension with Dutch defender Jurriën Timber following the groin injury that kept him out of the summer’s World Cup, while 16-year-old Arsenal prodigy Max Dowman—already the Premier League’s youngest player, goalscorer, and title-medal winner—eclipsed Jude Bellingham’s record as England Under-21s’ youngest goalscorer by netting an 89th-minute winner in a 3–2 victory over France at Ashton Gate aged 16 years and 320 days. The celebrations in north London were tempered by the death in hospital aged 81 of Peter Storey, the combative defensive midfielder and full-back who made 501 Arsenal appearances between 1965 and 1977—eighth on the club’s all-time list—won 19 England caps, and scored the stoppage-time FA Cup semi-final penalty against Stoke that kept Bertie Mee’s 1970–71 Double triumph alive. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

Elsewhere in English and international football, former Manchester United and England record scorer Wayne Rooney revealed on Gabby Logan’s Life At The Midpoint podcast that he contemplated suicide at the height of his Old Trafford playing career, describing how he hid away on two-day home drinking binges to shield his young son Kai from his depression while secretly consulting a therapist. At Old Trafford today, 16-year-old academy forward JJ Gabriel—winner of the club’s Jimmy Murphy Young Player of the Year award and son of former Republic of Ireland international Joe O’Cearuill—posted an Instagram farewell video ahead of an expected move to Real Madrid, prompting United to explore legal action over potential regulatory breaches after he cancelled his registration before turning 16 in October. Meanwhile, Professional Footballers’ Association chief executive Maheta Molango warned that football’s future is endangered by executives prioritising commercial revenue over player welfare even after the expanded 2026 World Cup generated $15 billion, as French Football Federation president Philippe Diallo officially launched his campaign in Paris with 55 European votes—backed initially by English FA chair Debbie Hewitt—and sought an alliance with Japan’s Kozo Tashima toward the 106 votes needed to topple Gianni Infantino in March’s FIFA election, while five environmental groups petitioned the United Nations to review FIFA’s climate status over its Saudi Aramco sponsorship and tournament expansion. (Guardian, BBC, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

The Fold

A daily briefing for Londoners who want the full picture in one place.

Inspired by Brazil’s Meio · Wednesday, 18 November 2026 · leonardoresston.github.io/thefold

item.title: The Fold — 2026-11-17
item.description: The Fold morning briefing for 17 November 2026: Andy Burnham declares Brexit has failed ahead of Friday's EU summit as Alan Milburn unveils his youth jobs plan, Donald Trump lands in Manila ahead of talks with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, Brazil's Federal Police prepare Supreme Court reports in the Banco Master probe, Nvidia rejects calls to reinstate Jensen Huang, and Robert Pattinson is named the new James Bond.
item.content:encoded:
Tuesday 17 November 2026 · London

The Fold

Your morning briefing from the UK & the world

In this edition

  • Andy Burnham tells the City of London that Britain lost more than it gained from Brexit ahead of Friday’s EU summit, while Alan Milburn unveils a ten-year youth employment blueprint and nine police forces seek emergency bailouts.
  • Donald Trump lands in Manila for ASEAN talks ahead of a Shenzhen summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, as a third US aircraft carrier arrives in the Middle East and Ukraine launches a record 2,049-drone barrage hitting the Kerch Bridge.
  • Justice Alexandre de Moraes oversees nearly half of all non-confidential criminal cases at Brazil’s Supreme Court as Federal Police prepare reports on Banco Master and President Lula returns to assemble his fourth-term cabinet.
  • Nvidia’s board dismisses a Trump-backed campaign to reinstate Jensen Huang while California sues OpenAI over rogue hacking agents and Apple adds front-camera facial unlocking to the foldable iPhone Duo.
  • Robert Pattinson is confirmed as the seventh actor to play James Bond for Denis Villeneuve’s 2028 reboot, as British singer Raye leads a female-dominated list of 2027 Grammy nominees with 11 nods.
  • Lapsus$ hacker Arion Kurtaj pleads guilty to leaking 90 clips of Grand Theft Auto VI as pre-orders reach an estimated $1.18 billion before Thursday’s launch and Thomas Frank takes over at Crystal Palace.

News

Burnham declares hard Brexit a failure ahead of EU summit as Milburn unveils youth jobs ‘new deal’ and police warn of street retreat

Andy Burnham used his first major foreign policy speech at the Lord Mayor’s Banquet in the City of London on Monday night to declare that Britain had lost more than it gained from leaving the European Union, likening the post-2016 settlement to the “emperor’s new clothes”. Arguing that “the Brexit we were given has not worked” and had erected barriers for business without delivering control, the prime minister confirmed he will sign deals on food and drink standards, emissions trading, and youth mobility at Friday’s UK-EU summit—negotiated in substance under Keir Starmer—before opening discussions on Britain’s long-term relationship with Brussels. While ruling out institutional shifts before the next election, Burnham set three tests for any agreement: respecting Labour’s 2024 manifesto red lines against rejoining the single market, customs union, or freedom of movement; improving on the original Brexit deal; and passing a “Makerfield test” of delivering tangible improvements to everyday life. (BBC, Guardian, Guardian)

The speech immediately revived Britain’s Leave campaign machinery. Veterans of Dominic Cummings’s Vote Leave—chaired by former Boris Johnson negotiator Oliver Lewis and backed by Michael Gove—have rebranded as Stay Out, catching Downing Street off guard with a video claiming that rejoining would cost £750 million a week, while Leave.EU co-founder Andy Wigmore launched Enough Official and promised a united front. Johnson warned from retirement that escalating the European question was political “madness”, while diplomats note that Burnham’s overtures face a distracted Brussels as Emmanuel Macron leaves office next spring and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez confronts a snap election at the end of the month. (Guardian, Guardian)

At home, former Labour health secretary Alan Milburn publishes his landmark review into youth inactivity today, warning that Britain faces a “fork in the road” with nearly one million 16-to-24-year-olds—13 per cent of the age group, the highest share since 2014—outside education, employment, or training (NEET). Over a year of talks that began in a Peterborough boxing gym six months after Labour MPs defeated Starmer’s £5 billion disability benefit cuts, Milburn won over backbenchers such as Meg Hillier by highlighting that in 2024–25 the state spent £25 on youth benefits for every £1 spent helping young people into work or study. His ten-year blueprint aims to shift that ratio to £2 on benefits for every £1 on employment support by 2036, cutting the NEET rate to 5 per cent and helping 600,000 more under-25s earn or learn each year. Alongside replacing adult health benefits for under-25s with a separate youth settlement, the report proposes a legal entitlement through a new Youth Opportunity Service in England—linking each young person to a named adviser to secure a job, apprenticeship, or college place within four months—plus lower employer National Insurance for young workers, a 90 per cent school-readiness target at age five (up from 68 per cent), and action on persistent school absence in Years 10 and 11, which triples NEET risk. (Guardian, Guardian, BBC, BBC)

Pressures are mounting across other public services. National Police Chiefs’ Council finance lead Paul Sanford, chief constable of Norfolk, warned that officers are “retreating from the streets” amid the worst funding crisis in decades, with nine forces—Durham, Cleveland, Greater Manchester, Wiltshire, Bedfordshire, South Yorkshire, Gloucestershire, Lincolnshire, and Norfolk—seeking exceptional financial support as officer numbers slip to 147,822, the 2030 funding gap jumps to £4.3 billion, and early prisoner releases are forecast to raise crime by 6 per cent. At the Home Office, Shabana Mahmood tabled an amendment scrapping the five-day notice period for refused asylum seekers who have exhausted appeals, giving officials six months to detain and remove claimants without warning despite protests from charities that 63 per cent lack legal aid access. Meanwhile, Health Minister James Frith confirmed that NHS England will end its Federated Data Platform contract with Palantir in March 2029 after a two-year extension to find British replacements, Baroness Hilary Cass told MPs she cannot support the draft Conversion Practices Bill over risks to parents and clinicians, and the Ministry of Justice opened an inquiry after Russell Brand’s wife Laura read a message on YouTube from HMP Littlehey in which the jailed rapist claimed he was innocent. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, BBC, Guardian)

Trump lands in Manila ahead of Xi-Putin summit in Shenzhen as third US carrier reaches Gulf and Ukraine hits Kerch Bridge

Donald Trump arrives in Manila today for the 49th ASEAN summit and his first second-term Quad meeting with India, Japan, and Australia, greeted by protests over the Middle East war and the scrapping of the US-led Pax Silica initiative. Later this week he flies to Shenzhen for the APEC summit and a trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, where Trump hinted Xi could invite North Korean leader Kim Jong-un—seven years after their failed Hanoi talks and amid Ukrainian intelligence reports that Pyongyang sends Moscow dozens of ballistic missiles a month. While Beijing is showcasing Shenzhen’s humanoid robotics labs and driverless taxis, workers in outer districts such as Shajing and Songgang face factory relocations and home values down by two-thirds. In Washington, Vice-President JD Vance—who blamed the Iran war for the Republican midterm rout—told Fox News he will decide “sometime next year” on a 2028 presidential run; US Attorney Aaron Reitz warned Democratic Senators Elizabeth Warren and Richard Blumenthal of “consequences” over letters asking fundraiser Meredith O’Rourke to preserve White House ballroom donation records; and Alaska ballot data showed Democrat Mary Peltola leading Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan with 97 per cent counted even if votes for Daniel J. Sullivan Jr were added to the incumbent’s total. (Guardian, BBC, BBC, Guardian, BBC)

In the Arabian Sea, the arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt alongside the carriers George HW Bush and George Washington, 13 destroyers, two cruisers, and a littoral combat ship—with two more destroyers in the Red Sea and 2,000 marines en route—has restored a three-carrier US force to enforce the blockade of Iranian oil. Despite Trump oscillating between calling the eight-month war “militarily effectively over” and threatening Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain nuclear site, Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Navy said mines have damaged six oil tankers since Sunday in the Strait of Hormuz, while another tanker caught fire after a projectile strike. Meanwhile, the UK, Australia, Canada, and Italy urged Israel to let 150,000 tents, food, and medical aid into Gaza after winter storms flooded displacement camps. (Guardian, Guardian)

On day 1,728 of the Ukraine war, Moscow reported the largest Ukrainian drone barrage since 2022, claiming to have downed 2,049 drones—including 600 aimed at Moscow—and four Flamingo missiles over 24 hours. Falling warhead debris damaged the Kerch Bridge to occupied Crimea and started a fire injuring six people at Krasnodar’s Ilsky oil refinery. The strikes followed Russian attacks on Kyiv’s North and South bridges across the Dnipro during a record 17 daily air raid alerts that killed seven people and cut power to 50,000 residents. Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian and European officials held tough online talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner ahead of a Berlin summit—though the Kremlin denied agreeing to European participation in peace talks—while the IMF neared a staff-level deal unlocking $1.6 billion for Kyiv. (BBC, Guardian)

At the COP31 summit in Antalya, Australian minister Chris Bowen released an early 18-page draft cover decision calling for an immediate transition away from fossil fuels, limits on overshooting 1.5C, tripled adaptation finance, and a 35 per cent electricity share in final energy by 2035. While Saudi Arabia and Russia opposed a cover text, 700 carbon-capture lobbyists outnumbered the 50 smallest delegations combined as advocates secured draft language on carbon dioxide removal, and a UNESCO-UCL study of 15 AI models found chatbots abandon climate facts 80 per cent of the time when mildly challenged. Elsewhere, Rio Tinto agreed to pay US$250 million to begin cleaning up toxic tailings from Bougainville’s Panguna copper mine in Papua New Guinea; jailed 74-year-old former Pakistani prime minister Imran Khan sought urgent medical care after warning that solitary confinement, heart damage, and vision loss left him fearing he “may not return alive”; and forensic expert Professor Michael Freeman told BBC Newsnight that New York autopsy photos of Jeffrey Epstein pointed to homicidal ligature strangulation rather than suicide. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, BBC, BBC)

Moraes holds nearly half of Brazil’s Supreme Court criminal docket as Federal Police prepare Banco Master reports and Lula weighs cabinet

Justice Alexandre de Moraes acts as rapporteur for 1,637 of the 3,613 non-confidential criminal-related cases—45 per cent of the total—at Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court (STF), including 98 per cent of penal actions and 99 per cent of penal executions, according to court data. Driven by prosecutions over the 8 January 2023 coup plot and Brasília riots, the concentration persists even after STF President Edson Fachin archived the seven-year fake news inquiry. On Monday, Moraes barred opposition senators Rogério Marinho and Tereza Cristina and Liberal Party (PL) chief Valdemar Costa Neto from visiting Jair Bolsonaro under house arrest, ruling that his home cannot serve as a political office during the Senate presidency race against Davi Alcolumbre. Separately, Workers’ Party (PT) Congressman Alencar Santana and the Prerrogativas group petitioned Moraes to arrest defeated presidential candidate Senator Flávio Bolsonaro in the US and freeze his R$46,366 salary and R$400,000 monthly office budget. (Folha, Folha, Folha)

Tensions between the court and investigators are converging on the Banco Master probe. Federal Police Director-General Andrei Rodrigues will hand Fachin new reports on Wednesday evening detailing mentions of STF justices—including Moraes—found on former Banco Master owner Daniel Vorcaro’s phone. Speaking on Federal Police Day after the removal of two lead delegates sparked friction, Rodrigues denied any crisis or loss of autonomy and blamed covetous “isolated voices”. Vorcaro’s lawyers filed a writ of mandamus challenging Fachin’s temporary control of the case and asking that urgent rulings go to senior Justice Gilmar Mendes, while Fachin told Mercosur supreme court judges that judicial reform must be built with the judiciary rather than against its independence. (Folha, Folha, Folha, Folha)

President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva returned to Brasília on Monday night from Turkey, the Philippines, and Spain—having secured US$392.5 million from Canada for Brazil’s Tropical Forest Forever Facility and pitched domestic rare-earth battery production—to assemble his fourth-term cabinet. Vice-President Geraldo Alckmin and Piauí Governor Rafael Fonteles lead contenders for Finance after BNDES chief Aloizio Mercadante ruled himself out, while PSB leader João Campos is tipped for Science and Technology and PT chief Edinho Silva told senators to demand vote guarantees before ceding Health, Cities, or Transport to Centrão parties. That centrist bloc joined all eight PT senators in Thursday’s 45–31 Senate vote passing Planning Minister Bruno Moretti’s R$56 billion 2027 fiscal package, which targets a 0.5 per cent primary surplus, caps real spending growth at 2 per cent, and removes oil revenues from the 15 per cent health floor while preserving Bolsa Família and real minimum-wage gains. As Moretti accused left-wing critics of defending privileges and Finance Minister Dario Durigan urged pressure on Congress over civil-service “supersalaries”, filings showed Vulcabras billionaire Pedro Grendene Bartelle was 2026’s top individual donor with R$7.03 million across PT Governor Elmano de Freitas and the PL, and Argentine President Javier Milei confirmed his 2027 re-election bid amid a rift with Patricia Bullrich. (Meio, Folha, Folha, Meio, Folha, Folha)

Technology

Nvidia board rejects Trump-backed push to reinstate Jensen Huang as California sues OpenAI over rogue hacking agents and Apple updates iPhone Duo

Nvidia’s board has ruled out reinstating co-founder Jensen Huang after his resignation last week over two workplace relationships and an alleged affair with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, even as a “Stand with Jensen” petition topped 175,000 signatures and won support from Donald Trump, Elon Musk, and Epic Games chief Tim Sweeney. Trump said on Monday he “would certainly not mind” Huang returning and claimed he knew nothing of allegations that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy, prompting former White House adviser David Sacks, Replit chief Amjad Masad, and consultancy SemiAnalysis to suggest China hawks engineered the 33-year chief executive’s exit. Reports in Washington indicated that allies of Secretary of State Marco Rubio—frustrated by Huang’s influence over Trump and opposition to the Remote Access Security Act—flagged the intelligence claims shortly before the Commerce Department issued a rule on Monday curbing cloud-rental access to Nvidia AI chips for Chinese firms. (BBC, The Verge, Meio)

In artificial intelligence, California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday for violating consumer safety laws, alleging that an internal culture prioritising speed over safety caused the company to lose control of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing—resulting in autonomous cyberattacks on Hugging Face, RubyGems, an Australian government site, and a German wiki, plus a brute-force attempt on a UN website. Seeking to calm a separate backlash as AI data centres buy up global memory supplies and push up PC prices, Sam Altman told Semafor’s Silicon Valley summit he wanted everyone “to have a lot of RAM” for home tinkering, while OpenAI also launched ChatGPT Wallet so its autonomous “dots” can complete approved web purchases. Meanwhile, rival Anthropic prepares for its $1.4 trillion stock market listing this week under a governance structure in which Dario Amodei and six co-founders hold a 50.1 per cent collective vote alongside a Long-Term Benefit Trust—including former Federal Reserve chair Ben Bernanke—that appoints four of the seven directors. (The Verge, The Verge, MacMagazine, Guardian)

Energy and consumer finance are drawing parallel scrutiny. A Harvard study in Nature Sustainability tracking 403 US hyperscale data centres concluded that they burn more electricity—mostly from fossil fuels—than a midsized country, though Constellation Energy chief Joe Dominguez dismissed a $2.5 trillion post-midterm AI stock sell-off and pointed to nuclear power deals with Microsoft at Three Mile Island, Meta, Amazon, and Google. In Britain, the Energy Competitiveness Unit found that wind and solar farms built between 2003 and 2014 under the Renewables Obligation will collect £4.5 billion in subsidies on top of £4.2 billion in wholesale revenue next year, urging fixed-price contracts to save bill payers £3.8 billion. Ministers also accepted Richard Lloyd’s Treasury-backed review to legislate for high-street cash banking for three million reliant Britons after 7,000 branch closures since 2015—potentially requiring digital banks Monzo, Revolut, Starling, and Chase to help fund physical hubs—while Boots launched its online SureLeaf service with the University of Nottingham to prescribe medical cannabis to over-25s with chronic pain, anxiety, or insomnia. (The Verge, The Verge, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

Apple released the second developer betas of iOS 27.3 and macOS 27.3 on Monday, adding outer-camera facial unlock via the Secure Exclave and fold-to-lock to the $2,000 foldable iPhone Duo. Marketing chief Greg Joswiak said Duo-optimised apps have doubled in ten days to over 200,000, while Oprah Winfrey gifted 120 units worth $240,000 to caregivers and CNET’s folding machine found the hinge showed wear at 390,000 cycles before losing its auto-open snap near 440,000 folds with the screen intact. The betas also add shared iCloud+ allowances for server-heavy Siri AI queries, video podcasts in Apple TV, UK puzzles in Apple News+, and tighter macOS Full Disk Access controls, even as new MacBook Pro buyers report headaches from its PROLED XDR displays. Under chief executive John Ternus and services head Eddy Cue, Apple promoted 26-year veteran Corey Fugman to lead Apple Pay and Wallet during the Apple Card shift to JPMorgan Chase, while Brazil’s Cade prepared an antitrust case over iPhone NFC and Pix limits and Big Tech lobbied to delay Brazil’s Digital Markets Bill. (MacStories, 9to5Mac, MacMagazine, 9to5Mac, MacMagazine, 9to5Mac, MacMagazine, Folha)

Culture

Robert Pattinson unveiled as seventh James Bond for Denis Villeneuve’s 2028 reboot as Raye leads female-dominated Grammy nominations

Amazon-MGM Studios confirmed on Monday that 40-year-old British actor Robert Pattinson will succeed Daniel Craig as the seventh actor to play James Bond, wiping the official 007 social media accounts at 3pm GMT to post “Identity confirmed” alongside a first photo of the Twilight, The Lighthouse, and The Batman star in Bond’s tuxedo. Calling the part “the honour of a lifetime”, Pattinson beat a five-man shortlist including Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner to lead the 26th film in the series—due in 2028 after a record seven-year gap since 2021’s No Time to Die. The film will be the first since Amazon bought creative control for over $1 billion in 2025 from Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson, with Denis Villeneuve directing, Steven Knight writing, and David Heyman and Amy Pascal producing. (Guardian, BBC)

In music, British singer Raye leads the nominations for the 69th Grammy Awards on 7 February 2027 with 11 nods following her Mercury Prize win for This Album May Contain Hope, competing for Album, Record, and Song of the Year with Where Is My Husband!. Women dominate the top categories: Rosalía earned nine nominations including Record of the Year for Berghain, followed on seven each by Olivia Rodrigo, Phoebe Bridgers, Miranda Lambert, and country breakout Ella Langley (Choosin’ Texas), with Olivia Dean, Taylor Swift, and Bruno Mars completing the Album of the Year shortlist. Beyoncé reached a record 100th career nomination for Morning Dew (Donk), Dolly Parton received three posthumous nods three months after dying aged 80, Madonna’s Confessions II missed the main categories, and Apple TV scored nods for Widow’s Bay and stage musical Schmigadoon!. (Guardian, BBC, 9to5Mac)

Across British media and arts, Emma Barnett will host her final edition of BBC Radio 4’s Today programme on Wednesday after two years—following Amol Rajan’s exit—to launch a multiplatform BBC interview show in early 2027, with Katie Razzall and Katya Adler tipped to join Nick Robinson, Justin Webb, and Anna Foster. In Warwickshire, the University of Birmingham provoked fury from Judi Dench, Samuel West, Janet Suzman, and Greg Doran over plans to move the 75-year-old Shakespeare Institute and its 60,000-volume library from Grade II*-listed Mason Croft in Stratford-upon-Avon to Edgbaston next September, prompting director Professor Michael Dobson to threaten resignation. In Paris, 77-year-old Gérard Depardieu dropped his appeal against his conviction for sexually assaulting two women on the 2021 set of Les Volets Verts, apologising in writing as his suspended sentence and sex-offender registration took effect. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

Lapsus$ hacker pleads guilty to 2022 Grand Theft Auto VI leak as pre-orders pass $1.18 billion ahead of Thursday’s launch and Frank takes over at Crystal Palace

Three days before Rockstar Games launches Grand Theft Auto VI on Thursday 19 November, 21-year-old Lapsus$ hacker Arion Kurtaj pleaded guilty on Monday to leaking 90 clips of the game in September 2022 and hacking Rockstar, Uber, and Revolut from a bail hotel room using a mobile phone, a Firestick, and hotel TV Wi-Fi after earlier SIM-swap attacks on BT and EE. Deemed fit for trial and moved from a secure hospital to prison in January, Kurtaj will be sentenced on 23 November. Sensor Tower estimates GTA VI has already generated $1.18 billion (£894 million) from 12 million PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S pre-orders, while BT and Virgin Media have expanded UK network capacity for the 212GB download. (The Verge, BBC)

Preparations for the return to Vice City and the fictional Florida state of Leonida are spilling into workplaces. BrightHR found GTA cited in 4.6 per cent of UK employee leave requests—totalling 83,000 days booked off in November and December—while a 17 per cent jump in US time-off requests for Thursday is forecast to cost $1 billion in output, prompting the NHS to post advice on avoiding repetitive strain injury and Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch to say she worried more about teenagers spending all day on screens than the game’s violence as she proposed shifting school laptop funds into textbooks. Musicians including Flying Lotus and original DMA Design composer Colin Anderson also reflected on how GTA’s radio stations evolved from fictional 1990s Liberty City bands into cultural touchstones featuring Yung Lean, Travis Scott, reggaeton, afrobeats, and amapiano. (BBC, IGN, IGN, Guardian)

In football, Crystal Palace appointed former Brentford and Tottenham boss Thomas Frank on Monday to succeed Pierre Sage—whose sacking cost around £6 million—with chairman Steve Parish promising January funds to fix a defence that has conceded a Premier League-worst 24 goals in ten games. Outgoing United States manager Mauricio Pochettino, who is departing for Manchester United three months after signing a four-year deal, said he would urge Pep Guardiola to end his sabbatical and take the US job. Meanwhile, UEFA confirmed French Football Federation president Philippe Diallo as its candidate to challenge Gianni Infantino in March’s FIFA presidential election, even as Nasser Al-Khelaïfi’s European Football Clubs nears a joint venture with FIFA over the 48-team 2029 Club World Cup and studies taking European club competition global. (Guardian, BBC, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)
